What are Monarch, Minister, Assistant and Guide?

The Monarch-Minister-Assistant-Guide principle is the core of formula composition in Chinese medicine, first recorded in the Huangdi Neijing (The Yellow Emperor\u0027s Classic of Medicine). It divides the herbs of a formula into four tiers by role — just as a state is governed through the division of duties, a formula works best when each herb plays its part and they cooperate with one another.

The Monarch herb is the leading herb of a formula, targeting the primary cause and mechanism of the illness. It carries the strongest force and is usually used in the largest amount; it is the indispensable core of the formula.
[In incense] The Monarch herb sets the direction of the whole blend — such as agarwood (chenxiang) in a calming blend, or musk in a refreshing one.
The Minister herb serves two purposes: first, it assists the Monarch in treating the main condition; second, it addresses accompanying symptoms. Its force is second only to the Monarch\u0027s.
[In incense] The Minister reinforces the Monarch — in a calming blend, agarwood leads as Monarch while sandalwood assists as Minister, deepening the calming effect.

The Assistant herb serves three purposes: it helps the Monarch and Minister strengthen the treatment; it restrains the toxicity or harshness of other herbs; and, where the condition demands, it may be opposite in nature to the Monarch yet complement it in effect.
[In incense] The Assistant balances the overall aroma — a touch of borneol or mint keeps the scent fresh and pleasant.
The Guide herb serves two purposes: it leads the other herbs to the affected area, and it harmonizes the formula so the herbs work in concert. It is usually used in small amounts.
[In incense] Herbs such as licorice act as Guides, harmonizing the aromas of all materials into one coherent scent.

The principle of Monarch-Minister-Assistant-Guide embodies the holistic and pattern-differentiated thinking of Chinese medicine. A fine formula is not a pile of herbs but a careful composition in which each herb gives its best and works with the others. Traditional incense follows the same rule: the Monarch sets the direction, the Minister adds strength, the Assistant restores balance, and the Guide harmonizes the whole — with all four in place, the blend becomes exquisite.
